lessons.title: What makes an element?

steps.headline: An element is set by its number of protons, called the atomic number.

lead.text: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. The number of protons is the atomic number, written Z.
Change Z and you have a different element. Every sodium atom has 11 protons; an atom with 12 is magnesium.
Both atoms are drawn with their particle counts. Only one of those counts names the element.

reveal.text: You read the atomic number from the protons alone. Oxygen has 8 of them, and the neutron and electron counts happened to match.

steps.headline: Neutrons and electrons can change while the element stays the same.

lead.text: A neutron adds mass to the nucleus but no charge, so the element is unchanged. An electron changes the charge but leaves the nucleus alone.

steps.headline: How many electrons does a neutral lithium atom have? Its atomic number is 3.

workedSteps.text: Atomic number 3 means 3 protons. Each carries +1.
A neutral atom has no overall charge, so the electrons must cancel that.
Each electron carries −1, so it takes 3 of them.

steps.headline: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?

workedSteps.text: Protons give the positive charge.
Count the electrons that cancel it.

lead.text: Neutrons do not count towards charge or identity.
An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons. Aluminium has atomic number 13.

lessons.orientation: Use protons to identify an element and separate identity from mass and charge.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Atom A has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. Atom B has 6 protons, 7 neutrons and 6 electrons. Both are carbon. Atom C has 7 protons, 7 neutrons and 7 electrons. It is not carbon.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell which element an atom is from its particle counts, and say what changes when neutrons or electrons do.

recap.keyIdea: An element is set by its proton count, the atomic number. Neutrons change an atom's mass and electrons change its charge, but neither changes the element.

blocks.text: You saw that two carbon atoms can differ in neutrons and still be carbon. You found that a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, and that a nucleus holds only protons and neutrons.

recap.nextHook: Atoms of one element can still differ in mass. Next: how many neutrons, and what that does to mass.

lessons.title: Same element, different mass

steps.headline: The mass number counts the protons and neutrons together.

lead.text: Protons and neutrons each weigh about 1 u, and electrons weigh almost nothing. So the particle count of the nucleus is a good label for an atom's mass.
That count is the mass number, A. It goes after the name: carbon-13 has A = 13.

steps.headline: Sodium-23 has atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?

workedSteps.text: The mass number is the protons plus the neutrons.
Move the protons across to leave the neutrons.
Put in A = 23 and Z = 11.

steps.headline: Find the neutrons in an atom of chlorine-35, atomic number 17.

workedSteps.text: Mass number and atomic number are given.
Work out N = A − Z.

steps.headline: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

lead.text: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 both have 17 protons, so both are chlorine. One has two more neutrons, so it is heavier.
Same element, different mass: that is what makes them isotopes.
Use the same move as before: the mass number minus the protons leaves the neutrons.

steps.headline: A sample's average mass is a weighted average of its isotopes.

lead.text: A real sample holds billions of atoms, often of more than one isotope. The average mass of an atom in it falls between the isotope masses, nearer the more common one.
Take a sample with equal numbers of two kinds of atom. The average is the mean of their masses.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish mass number, isotopes and the average mass of a mixture.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: One carbon atom has 12 particles in its nucleus. Another carbon atom has 14 particles in its nucleus.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an atom's neutrons from its mass number, and say why one element can have atoms of different mass.

recap.keyIdea: Mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share a proton count but differ in neutrons, so an element's average atomic mass is a weighted average of its isotopes.

blocks.text: You found 18 neutrons in chlorine-35 and 22 in potassium-41 by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number. You also saw that equal numbers of 12 u and 14 u atoms average 13 u.

recap.nextHook: Neutrons are only one thing that can change. Next: what happens when an atom gains or loses electrons.

lessons.title: Gaining and losing electrons

steps.headline: An ion is an atom with unequal protons and electrons, and its charge is protons minus electrons.

lead.text: A neutral atom has equal numbers of the two. Give it a different number of electrons and it becomes an ion.
Count each proton as +1 and each electron as −1. The charge is the protons minus the electrons.

steps.headline: A magnesium ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?

workedSteps.text: Charge is protons minus electrons.
There are more protons, so the positive charges win.

steps.headline: An oxide ion has 8 protons and 10 electrons. Find its charge.

workedSteps.text: Subtract the electrons from the protons.
Say what the charge is, with its sign.

steps.headline: Electrons move in and out of an atom, but its nucleus never changes.

lead.text: Losing electrons takes away negative charge, so the ion is positive. Gaining them makes it negative.
Ordinary chemistry moves electrons only. The protons stay, so the element stays.
Write the two counts down with the protons first, then subtract.
Aluminium commonly forms an ion by losing three electrons. Compare its protons with its electrons now.

lessons.orientation: Calculate ion charge while keeping element identity unchanged.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A neutral atom has 5 protons and 5 electrons. Then it gains 3 more electrons.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out an ion's charge from its protons and electrons, and say what stays the same.

recap.keyIdea: An ion's charge is its proton count minus its electron count. Gaining electrons makes it negative and losing them makes it positive. The element never changes.

blocks.text: You found that 12 protons and 10 electrons give +2, and 8 protons with 10 electrons give −2. Every time, you subtracted the electrons from the protons.

recap.nextHook: Electrons are not all alike: the outer ones decide how an atom behaves. Next: which electrons sit on the outside.

lessons.title: The outer electrons

steps.headline: Electrons sit in shells, and the shells fill from the inside: 2, then 8, then 8.

lead.text: The first shell holds up to 2 electrons. The second and third hold up to 8 each, for the first eighteen elements.
In a drawing, each circle groups the electrons of one shell. Electrons do not run along the circles.
Neutral oxygen has 8 electrons in total. Fill the first shell, then see how many are left.

reveal.text: You filled the first shell with 2 and carried the rest outwards. Whatever is left sits in the outer shell.

steps.headline: The electrons in the outermost occupied shell are the valence electrons.

lead.text: Chemical behaviour is decided at the outside of an atom, so those electrons get their own name. Find the last shell that has any electrons in it and count them.

steps.headline: Neutral silicon has 14 electrons. How many are valence electrons?

workedSteps.text: Fill the first shell with 2.
The second shell takes up to 8, and no more.
The 4 left sit in the third shell, the last one used. They are the valence electrons.

steps.headline: Neutral magnesium has 12 electrons. Find its valence electrons.

workedSteps.text: Fill the first shell with 2.
Fill the second shell with 8, then see what is left.

lead.text: Fill each shell in turn and see what is left over.
Helium has only one shell, so the rule for the second shell never reaches it.

lessons.orientation: Read shell populations for the first eighteen elements and identify valence electrons.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A theatre has a front row of 2 seats, a second row of 8 and a third row of 8. Nine people arrive and fill the rows from the front, each row full before the next one starts.

intro.promise: By the end you'll place an atom's electrons in shells and pick out the outer ones.

recap.keyIdea: Electrons fill shells from the inside: 2, then 8, then 8. The electrons in the last occupied shell are the valence electrons, and they decide how an atom behaves.

blocks.text: You filled shells for silicon and magnesium by taking 2, then 8, off the total. The electrons left over were the outer ones, and neon's last shell came out full.

recap.nextHook: Atoms with a nearly empty or nearly full outer shell can swap electrons. Next: how that builds a neutral ionic formula.

lessons.title: Making a neutral formula

steps.headline: An ionic compound has no overall charge, so its ions come in a ratio that cancels.

lead.text: Positive and negative ions attract and stack into a crystal. The crystal as a whole is neutral, so the charges must add to zero.
The formula records the ratio. A subscript says how many of that ion there are.

steps.headline: Na⁺ and S²⁻ form a compound. What is its formula?

workedSteps.text: Write the charges: +1 on each sodium ion, −2 on each sulfide ion.
One Na⁺ cancels only half of the −2, so you need two of them.
Write the counts as subscripts. A 1 is left out.

steps.headline: Aluminium oxide is built from Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Find the ratio.

workedSteps.text: Three O²⁻ ions bring a total charge of −6.
Find how many Al³⁺ ions bring +6.

lead.text: Find the smallest whole numbers of each ion whose charges cancel.

steps.headline: A formula unit is the simplest ratio of ions in the crystal, not a separate molecule.

lead.text: An ionic crystal runs on through enormous numbers of ions. NaCl records the ratio of the whole crystal. It does not describe a pair of atoms floating inside it.
Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. Write the simplest formula unit.

lessons.orientation: Find whole-number ion ratios that balance electric charge.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a card game, one card scores +6 and the other cards each score −2. A hand wins when its cards total zero.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the simplest neutral formula for an ionic compound from the charges on its ions.

recap.keyIdea: An ionic compound is neutral, so its ions come in the smallest whole-number ratio whose charges add to zero. The formula writes that ratio, not a separate molecule.

blocks.text: You balanced +2 with two −1 ions, +6 with three −2 ions, and found that Ca²⁺ with N³⁻ takes three calcium to two nitrogen. Each time the charges added to zero.

recap.nextHook: Not every bond hands electrons over. Next: atoms that share electron pairs instead.

lessons.title: Sharing electron pairs

steps.headline: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms.

lead.text: Some atoms are close to a full outer shell and share rather than swap. Both atoms count the shared pair as their own.
In a Lewis drawing each bond line is one shared pair.
Hydrogen, H₂, is drawn with a single line between its atoms.

reveal.text: You turned one line into one pair, and one pair into its electrons. That is all a single bond is.

steps.headline: Carbon dioxide has two double bonds. How many electrons are shared altogether?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.
Each pair holds two electrons, so count in pairs first and then double.
There are two double bonds.

steps.headline: Oxygen, O₂, has one double bond. How many electrons does it share?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.
Turn the pairs into electrons.

steps.headline: A shared pair counts for both atoms, while a lone pair stays on one atom.

lead.text: Not every outer electron is shared. Electrons that stay on one atom, as a pair, are lone pairs. They are drawn as two dots.
A shared pair is still only one pair in the molecule, even though both atoms count it.
Ethene, C₂H₄, has one double bond between the carbons and four single C–H bonds.
Nitrogen, N₂, is held together by a triple bond.

lessons.orientation: Read single, double and triple bonds and distinguish shared electrons from lone pairs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two chlorine atoms each have 7 outer electrons. Each puts one electron into a pair that both atoms count as their own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the shared and unshared electrons in a Lewis drawing.

recap.keyIdea: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons that both atoms count toward their shells. More bond lines mean more shared pairs, and lone pairs stay with one atom.

blocks.text: You counted 4 shared electrons in O₂, 8 across the two double bonds in CO₂ and 12 in ethene. Each time you took pairs first and then doubled.

recap.nextHook: A formula only lists atoms. Next: how to read the subscripts and coefficients in a chemical formula.

lessons.title: Reading a chemical formula

steps.headline: A subscript counts atoms in one unit, and a coefficient counts how many units.

lead.text: The small number after a symbol is a subscript. In H₂O it says there are two H atoms in each molecule, and no number means one.
A big number in front is a coefficient. It counts whole molecules: 2 H₂O is two molecules.
Look at the three water molecules and decide what to count.

reveal.text: You took the oxygen in one molecule and counted it once per molecule. That is what a coefficient asks for.

steps.headline: How many hydrogen atoms are in 4 H₂SO₄?

workedSteps.text: Read the subscript: each H₂SO₄ has 2 H atoms.
Read the coefficient: there are 4 units.
Multiply the atoms in one unit by the units.

steps.headline: Count the oxygen atoms in 2 Al₂O₃.

workedSteps.text: The subscript after O is 3, so each unit has 3 oxygen atoms.
Multiply by the 2 units.

steps.headline: Change a coefficient to change the amount. Changing a subscript changes the substance.

lead.text: Change H₂O to H₂O₂ and you have hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. To have more water without changing it, write a bigger number in front.
Add up the atoms of every element in one unit first, then multiply by the units.
Ammonia is NH₃. A missing subscript means one atom.

lessons.orientation: Separate subscripts inside a formula from coefficients multiplying whole units.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A sandwich box holds 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. You buy 5 boxes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the atoms of each element in something like 3 H₂O.

recap.keyIdea: A subscript counts the atoms of an element in one unit, and a coefficient counts the units. Multiply the two to count the atoms.

blocks.text: You counted hydrogen in 4 H₂SO₄, oxygen in 2 Al₂O₃ and every atom in 2 H₂SO₄. Each time you took the atoms in one unit and multiplied by the units.

recap.nextHook: Once you can count atoms, you can add up their masses. Next: the mass of one formula unit.

lessons.title: Adding atomic masses

steps.headline: Formula mass is the total of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula.

lead.text: Each element has an atomic mass, measured in u. To get the mass of a whole formula, multiply each element's mass by its atom count from the subscripts, then add the results.
For these estimates use H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u and O = 16 u.
Water is H₂O. Count the hydrogen atoms and the oxygen atoms, then use their masses.

reveal.text: You added the hydrogen's mass twice and the oxygen's once, which is what the subscripts ask for.

steps.headline: Using S = 32 u and O = 16 u, find the formula mass of SO₂.

workedSteps.text: Count the atoms: one S and two O.
The oxygen mass is counted once for each oxygen atom.
Work it out.

steps.headline: Using C = 12 u and O = 16 u, find the formula mass of CO₂.

workedSteps.text: Count the atoms: one C and two O.
Work out the total.

steps.headline: Use the atomic masses a problem states, because they are rounded.

lead.text: Real atomic masses are averages over isotopes, so chlorine's is about 35.5 u, not a whole number. A problem tells you which values to use, so everyone gets the same answer.
Use Ca = 40 u, C = 12 u and O = 16 u. Count each element's atoms before you add.
Use Mg = 24 u and Cl = 35.5 u. An ionic solid has a formula mass too.

lessons.orientation: Build formula mass from atom counts and stated rounded atomic masses.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pack holds 2 tennis balls of 60 g each and 1 golf ball of 45 g.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the formula mass of a compound from its formula and the atomic masses you are given.

recap.keyIdea: Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula. Multiply each element's atomic mass by its atom count, then add.

blocks.text: You found 64 u for SO₂, 44 u for CO₂ and 100 u for CaCO₃. Each time you multiplied each atom's mass by its count and added the results.

recap.nextHook: A formula mass is for one unit. Next: the mole, which turns it into grams for a whole sample.

lessons.title: From moles to mass

steps.headline: A mole is a fixed, very large count, in the way a dozen is 12.

lead.text: One mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ entities. Always say what you are counting, because one mole of anything is that same number of that thing.
The mass of one mole is the molar mass, M, in g/mol.
Use M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol, the mass of one mole of water. Then think about two moles.

reveal.text: You scaled the mass of one mole by the number of moles. That is the rule m = n × M.

steps.headline: Using M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol, find the mass of 2 mol of sodium chloride.

workedSteps.text: Mass is the amount times the molar mass.
Each mole has the molar mass, so more moles means proportionally more mass.
Work it out.

steps.headline: Using M(N₂) = 28 g/mol, find the mass of 2 mol of nitrogen.

workedSteps.text: Mass is the amount times the molar mass.
Put the numbers in and work it out.

steps.headline: To find an amount from a mass, divide by the molar mass.

lead.text: Run the conversion backwards: n = m ÷ M. A mass equal to M is exactly one mole.
Use the backwards rule: divide the mass by the mass of one mole.
The ratio in a formula also works for moles. One mole of NH₃ molecules holds one mole of N atoms and some moles of H atoms.

lessons.orientation: Convert between amount and mass while identifying what one mole counts.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: One dozen bolts has a mass of 150 g.

intro.promise: By the end you'll convert between moles and grams, and say what a mole counts.

recap.keyIdea: A mole is a fixed count of entities, and molar mass is the mass of one mole. Mass is amount times molar mass, so amount is mass divided by molar mass.

blocks.text: You found 117 g for 2 mol of NaCl and 56 g for 2 mol of N₂, then worked back to 5 mol in 90 g of water. The same one-mole mass did both jobs.

recap.nextHook: Now you can count and weigh. Next: writing a reaction so that every atom is accounted for.

lessons.title: Keep every atom

steps.headline: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

lead.text: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction. None are created or destroyed.
In 2 Li + F₂ → 2 LiF there are two Li and two F on each side, so the equation is balanced.
Count the oxygen atoms in the product first, then ask how many O₂ molecules supply them.

reveal.text: You matched oxygen on both sides by working out how many O₂ molecules supply those atoms. That is balancing.

steps.headline: Balance ? K + Cl₂ → 2 KCl. What goes before K?

workedSteps.text: Count chlorine. The product has 2 Cl, and Cl₂ on the left has 2.
Count potassium. The product has 2 K, so the left needs 2.
Write the coefficient in front of K. Never touch the subscripts.

steps.headline: Balance CH₄ + ? O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What goes before O₂?

workedSteps.text: Count oxygen on the right: 2 in CO₂ and 2 in the waters.
Find how many O₂ molecules supply that many O atoms.

steps.headline: Balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts.

lead.text: A coefficient changes how many molecules there are. A subscript changes which substance it is: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water.
Count each element on the right first, then match the left.
Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen. Balance the hydrogen by counting the atoms in the ammonia.

lessons.orientation: Balance reactions by changing coefficients while preserving chemical formulas.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Each toy car needs 4 wheels. You build 3 cars. The wheels come only in packs of 2.

intro.promise: By the end you'll balance a simple reaction by choosing coefficients so that every atom is accounted for.

recap.keyIdea: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. You balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts.

blocks.text: You balanced the O₂ in methane burning, the H₂ in making ammonia and the Mg in making magnesium oxide. Each time you counted one element at a time and adjusted a coefficient.

recap.nextHook: A balanced equation is also a recipe. Next: using its coefficients as ratios between amounts.

lessons.title: Read a reaction as a ratio

steps.headline: The coefficients in a balanced equation are a ratio of amounts in moles.

lead.text: Read 2 K + Br₂ → 2 KBr as a recipe in moles: the coefficients 2, 1 and 2 are the amounts of K, Br₂ and KBr.
Scale all three by the same factor and the equation still holds. That is a mole ratio.
Compare the ammonia coefficient with the nitrogen coefficient. Excess hydrogen means nitrogen is the only limit.

reveal.text: You used the ratio of the two coefficients, scaled to your amount. That is every mole calculation from an equation.

steps.headline: For 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl, how many moles of Cl₂ are needed for 5 mol of Na?

workedSteps.text: Take the ratio from the coefficients: 1 Cl₂ for every 2 Na.
Multiply by a factor with Na underneath, so the Na cancels.
workedSteps.math: 5 mol Na × (1 mol Cl₂ / 2 mol Na)

workedSteps.text: Work it out.

steps.headline: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of water form from 3 mol of O₂ with excess H₂?

workedSteps.text: The ratio is 2 mol H₂O for every 1 mol O₂.
workedSteps.math: 3 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂)

workedSteps.text: Work out the amount of water.

steps.headline: Coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios.

lead.text: One mole of each substance has its own mass, so grams do not follow the coefficients. Change masses to moles first, then use the ratio.
Read the ratio of O₂ to Mg from the coefficients, then scale it.
The ratio depends on which substance you start from and which you want. Here you start from methane and want oxygen.

lessons.orientation: Use balanced coefficients to convert between reacting and produced amounts.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read a reaction as a ratio
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pancake recipe uses 2 eggs for every 8 pancakes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a balanced equation to say how many moles of one substance go with another.

recap.keyIdea: The coefficients of a balanced equation are a ratio of amounts in moles, not of masses. Multiply the amount you have by the coefficient ratio to find the amount you want.

blocks.text: You found 2.5 mol of Cl₂ for 5 mol of Na, 6 mol of water from 3 mol of O₂ and 4 mol of O₂ for 2 mol of methane. Each time you scaled by a ratio taken from the coefficients.

recap.nextHook: A ratio assumes enough of everything. Next: what happens when one reactant runs out first.

lessons.title: The reactant that runs out

steps.headline: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets how much product forms.

lead.text: One batch of a reaction uses the coefficients as amounts: one batch of 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O uses 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂.
A supply can run only so many batches. The reactant that allows the fewest is limiting, and the others are in excess.
One batch uses 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂. Work out how many batches each supply could run.

reveal.text: You compared how many batches each supply allows. What was left of the other reactant made no difference to the product.

steps.headline: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, start with 5 mol N₂ and 6 mol H₂. How much NH₃ can form?

workedSteps.text: Divide each amount by its coefficient to count batches.
Take the smaller number. That reactant runs out first.
Each batch forms 2 mol of NH₃.

steps.headline: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, start with 4 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂. How much NH₃ can form?

workedSteps.text: Count the batches each supply allows.
Use the smaller count, times 2 mol NH₃ per batch.

steps.headline: The excess reactant is only partly used, and the rest is left over.

lead.text: The limiting reactant sets how many batches happen. Work out how much of the excess reactant those batches use, then subtract that from what you started with.
Find the limiting reactant first. Then see how much of the other one the batches use.
The same method works for any reaction. Here the supplies are 3 mol CH₄ and 4 mol O₂.

lessons.orientation: Find theoretical products and leftovers by comparing available amounts with the reaction ratio.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A sandwich needs 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. You have 9 slices of bread and 5 slices of cheese.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find which reactant runs out first and how much product forms.

recap.keyIdea: The reactant that supports the fewest batches of the reaction is limiting. It sets the theoretical yield, and the other reactants are left over.

blocks.text: You found 4 mol of NH₃ from 5 mol N₂ and 6 mol H₂ by comparing batches, and 0.5 mol of O₂ left from 3 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂. Each time the smaller batch count set the answer.

recap.nextHook: That is the theoretical amount. Real reactions fall short of it, which is the idea of percentage yield for a later course.

questions.prompt: Oxygen has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: Choose the particle that identifies the element.
Z counts protons; it ignores neutrons and electrons.
Which supplied count is the definition of atomic number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Atomic number counts protons, so Z = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. The atomic number is the proton count, whatever the neutrons and electrons are doing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the neutrons. The atomic number counts one kind of particle only.

questions.prompt: The two carbon cases differ in neutron count. Why are they both carbon?
hints: Compare the nuclei's proton counts.

acceptedIdeas: Their proton counts agree
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each nucleus still contains six protons.

choices.label: Their proton counts agree
Their masses agree
Their total particle counts agree

questions.onCorrect: Same proton count, same element. The extra neutron changes the mass, not the identity.

misconceptions.feedback: The masses differ here: one has an extra neutron. Look for the count that stays fixed.
The totals differ, because one nucleus has an extra neutron. Look for what stays fixed.

questions.prompt: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?
hints: Neutral means no net electric charge.
Each proton is +1 and each electron is −1.
How many negative charges cancel the nucleus's positive charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven electrons cancel the charge of seven protons.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Seven electrons cancel the charge of seven protons, so a neutral atom has equal counts.

The equation gives two ammonia moles per nitrogen mole.
Evaluate 2 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 mol N₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 1 mol N₂) = 4 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The equation gives two NH₃ for each N₂, so double the nitrogen amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The ratio of NH₃ to N₂ is more than one to one.
That is the amount of nitrogen. The equation gives more ammonia than nitrogen.

questions.prompt: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of water can 3 mol O₂ form with excess H₂?
hints: Each mole of oxygen supports two moles of water.
The equation gives two water moles per oxygen mole.
Evaluate 3 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The water-to-oxygen ratio is 2:1, giving 6 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 6 mol. Each O₂ makes two H₂O, so triple the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen amount. Each O₂ makes more than one H₂O.
That divides by the ratio. Multiply by the ratio of water to oxygen.

questions.prompt: The coefficients 1:3:2 in N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ directly give which ratio?
hints: Keep the amount unit attached to the ratio.

acceptedIdeas: Moles of the three substances
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coefficients count entities and amounts in moles; masses require molar masses.

choices.label: Grams of the three substances
Moles of the three substances
Their temperatures

questions.onCorrect: Coefficients are ratios of amounts in moles. Masses need the molar masses as well.

misconceptions.feedback: Grams need molar masses. Coefficients count amounts.
Coefficients say nothing about temperature.

questions.prompt: For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, how many moles of O₂ are required by 2 mol CH₄?
hints: Read oxygen required per methane consumed.
The oxygen-to-methane coefficient ratio is 2:1.
Evaluate 2 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 × 2 = 4 mol O₂.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The ratio is two O₂ for each CH₄, so double the methane amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The ratio is not one to one. Each CH₄ needs more than one O₂.
That is the methane amount. Scale it by the ratio.

questions.prompt: For 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, how many moles of MgO can 4 mol Mg form with excess oxygen?
hints: Reduce the product-to-reactant coefficient ratio.
The magnesium and magnesium oxide coefficients are both two.
Equal reactant and product coefficients keep the molar amount unchanged.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The Mg-to-MgO ratio is 2:2, or 1:1.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The ratio of MgO to Mg is 1 : 1, so the amount is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the amount, but the Mg and MgO coefficients match.
That doubles the amount, but the Mg and MgO coefficients match.

questions.prompt: A stoichiometric calculation predicts 10 mol of product. When is this theoretical amount reached?
hints: Separate a theoretical calculation from actual reaction yield.

acceptedIdeas: When the stated reaction completes without competing losses
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The theoretical amount assumes the limiting reactant follows the stated reaction completely.

choices.label: Whenever the drawing is balanced
When the stated reaction completes without competing losses
Only if all coefficients equal one

questions.onCorrect: A theoretical amount assumes the reaction goes as written, to completion and with no losses.

misconceptions.feedback: Balance is necessary, but real reactions can still lose product.
The coefficients can be any whole numbers. They do not set the yield.

questions.prompt: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, start with 6 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂. What is the theoretical water yield in mol?
hints: Divide each available amount by its coefficient, then choose the smaller result.
The supplies support 6/2 and 1/1 reaction batches.
Use the water coefficient to turn the smaller batch count into product amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: O₂ supports one batch, producing 2 mol H₂O.

questions.onCorrect: 2 mol. Oxygen allows one batch, and each batch forms two waters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the batches the hydrogen would allow, but the oxygen runs out earlier.
That is the hydrogen supply. The product is set by the reactant that runs out first.

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, start with 4 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂. Find the theoretical NH₃ yield in mol.
hints: Nitrogen alone could react farther, but hydrogen cannot.
The supplies support 4/1 and 3/3 reaction batches.
Use the ammonia coefficient to turn the smaller batch count into product amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hydrogen supports one batch, producing 2 mol NH₃.

questions.onCorrect: 2 mol. Hydrogen allows only one batch, and each batch forms two NH₃.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen supply. Each batch forms two NH₃.
Nitrogen alone would allow more, but hydrogen runs out first.

questions.prompt: How do you identify a limiting reactant from given molar amounts?
hints: Compare both supplies on the same reaction scale.

acceptedIdeas: Choose the smaller amount divided by its coefficient
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Available amount divided by coefficient measures how far each supply lets the reaction proceed.

choices.label: Choose the smaller coefficient
Choose the smaller amount divided by its coefficient
Choose the heavier molecule

questions.onCorrect: Divide each amount by its coefficient. The reactant with the smaller result runs out first.

misconceptions.feedback: The coefficient alone does not say which supply runs out. Compare amounts per batch.
Molar mass does not decide which reactant runs out.

questions.prompt: For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, start with 3 mol CH₄ and 4 mol O₂. Find the theoretical water yield in mol.
hints: Use two oxygen moles for each reaction batch.
The supplies support 3/1 and 4/2 reaction batches.
Use the water coefficient to turn the smaller batch count into product amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Oxygen supports two batches, each producing 2 mol water: 4 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. Oxygen allows two batches, and each batch forms two waters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the methane supply. Oxygen runs out first.
That would need more oxygen than there is.

questions.prompt: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, start with 6 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂. How many moles of H₂ remain after complete reaction?
hints: Subtract the reacted amount from the supply.
One mole of oxygen reacts with two moles of hydrogen.
Subtract the two reacted hydrogen moles from the initial six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One mole O₂ consumes two moles H₂, leaving 6 − 2 = 4 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. One mole of O₂ uses two moles of H₂, so the rest is left over.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hydrogen used, not what remains.
That is the amount you started with. Some of it reacted.

questions.prompt: If reactants are supplied in the exact balanced ratio and react completely, what remains?
hints: Compare available amount divided by coefficient for both reactants.

acceptedIdeas: No excess reactant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both supplies are consumed together in the required ratio.

choices.label: A fixed half of each reactant
No excess reactant
The reactant with the larger molar mass

questions.onCorrect: Both supplies run out together, so nothing is left of either reactant.

misconceptions.feedback: No fixed share is left. Exact ratios use up both reactants.
Molar mass does not decide what remains.

questions.prompt: What is the mass of the whole pack, in grams?
hints: How much do the two tennis balls weigh together?
Then add the golf ball.
Two lots of the tennis ball's mass, plus one lot of the golf ball's.
questions.onCorrect: 165 g. Multiply each kind's mass by how many there are, then add. A formula mass works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one tennis ball. The pack holds more than one.
That leaves out the golf ball.

questions.prompt: Using N = 14 u, find the formula mass of N₂ in u.
hints: Read the subscript after N.
That is how many nitrogen atoms there are.
Multiply that count by the mass of one atom.
questions.onCorrect: 28 u. The subscript counts the atoms, and each adds its mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one atom's mass. The subscript says there are more than one.

questions.prompt: Why is the oxygen mass counted twice in SO₂?

acceptedIdeas: The subscript says there are two oxygen atoms, and each adds its mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two O atoms, 16 u each.

choices.label: The subscript says there are two oxygen atoms, and each adds its mass
Oxygen is always heavier than sulfur
The mass of a compound is double its atomic masses

questions.onCorrect: Right: each atom adds its own mass, so two oxygen atoms add twice.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is lighter than sulfur here. The count of atoms matters.
Formula mass is not doubled. It adds the masses of the atoms present.

questions.prompt: Using Ca = 40 u, C = 12 u and O = 16 u, find the formula mass of CaCO₃ in u.
hints: Count the atoms of each element from the subscripts.
Three oxygen atoms, one of each other element.
Evaluate 40 + 12 + 3 × 16.
questions.onCorrect: 100 u. One Ca, one C and three O atoms, each adding its mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one oxygen atom. The subscript says there are three.
That leaves out the oxygen atoms.

questions.prompt: Using Na = 23 u, O = 16 u and H = 1 u, find the formula mass of NaOH in u.
hints: Which elements are in NaOH, and how many atoms of each?
No subscripts, so one of each.
Add the three masses.
questions.onCorrect: 40 u. One atom of each element, so add the three atomic masses.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the hydrogen. Every atom in the formula counts.

questions.prompt: How many packs of wheels do you need?
hints: How many wheels do 3 cars need in total?
Each pack holds the same number of wheels.
Divide the wheels needed by the wheels in a pack.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 × 4 = 12 wheels, and 12 ÷ 2 = 6 packs.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Work out what you need, then how many of the pack supplies it. Balancing an equation asks the same thing of atoms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of wheels. The wheels come in packs.
That is the number of cars. Count the wheels first.

questions.prompt: In 2 Li + F₂ → 2 LiF, how many F atoms are on the right-hand side?
hints: The number in front multiplies the whole formula.
How many F atoms are in one LiF?
Multiply the coefficient by the F atoms in one unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 LiF × 1 F each = 2 F.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the F in one LiF. The coefficient multiplies it.
That counts the Li atoms as well. The question asks about F.

questions.prompt: Why must we not change KCl to K₂Cl to balance?

acceptedIdeas: Changing a subscript makes a different substance, so only coefficients may change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: K₂Cl is not potassium chloride.

choices.label: Changing a subscript makes a different substance, so only coefficients may change
Subscripts are always correct in any compound
K₂Cl would have too many chlorine atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: the formula names the substance, and only coefficients change how much of it there is.

misconceptions.feedback: Subscripts come from the substance, which is why we do not edit them to balance.
The issue is not the number of atoms. K₂Cl is simply not the substance we started with.

questions.prompt: Balance ? Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃. What coefficient belongs before Al?
hints: Count the Al atoms in the product.
Each AlCl₃ holds one Al.
Match the Al atoms on the left to the right.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 AlCl₃ hold 2 Al, so the left needs 2 Al.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The product has two Al atoms, so the left needs two.

misconceptions.feedback: One Al would give one Al atom, but the product has more.
That is the coefficient of Cl₂. Match the aluminium atoms.

questions.prompt: Balance 2 C₂H₆ + ? O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 6 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Count the O atoms in 4 CO₂.
Add the O atoms in 6 H₂O.
Divide the total O atoms by the atoms in one O₂.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The products hold 14 O atoms, and each O₂ supplies two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of O atoms needed. Each O₂ supplies two of them.
That counts only the oxygen in the CO₂. The waters hold oxygen too.

questions.prompt: What is the mass of 4 dozen of the bolts, in grams?
hints: Each dozen has the same mass.
Four dozen is four lots of that mass.
Multiply the mass of one dozen by the number of dozens.
questions.onCorrect: 600 g. A fixed count has a fixed mass, so more counts mean proportionally more mass. A mole works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one dozen. You have more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the mass of one dozen by the number of dozens.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the amount by the molar mass?

acceptedIdeas: Each mole has the molar mass, so more moles have proportionally more mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two moles weigh twice as much as one.

choices.label: Each mole has the molar mass, so more moles have proportionally more mass
The molar mass is the number of moles in a gram
Multiplying converts grams into molecules

questions.onCorrect: Right: the mass of one mole, repeated for each mole.

misconceptions.feedback: Molar mass is grams per mole, not moles per gram.
Counting molecules is a different step. This one finds a mass.

questions.prompt: Using M(N₂) = 28 g/mol, find the mass of 2 mol of nitrogen in grams.
hints: Use m = n × M.
Put in the amount and the molar mass.
Evaluate 2 × 28.
questions.onCorrect: 56 g. The amount times the molar mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass of one mole. There are more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: Using M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol, how many moles are in 90 g of water?
hints: Which rule finds an amount from a mass?
Divide the mass by the molar mass.
How many lots of 18 g fit into 90 g?
questions.onCorrect: 5 mol. Divide the mass by the mass of one mole.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two. To find an amount, divide the mass by the molar mass.
That divides the molar mass by the mass, the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: How many moles of oxygen atoms are in 3 mol of CO₂ molecules?
hints: How many O atoms are in one CO₂ molecule?
The same ratio holds for moles.
Multiply the moles of CO₂ by the O atoms per molecule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 × 2 = 6 mol of O atoms.

questions.onCorrect: 6 mol. Two O atoms per molecule, so twice the moles of CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen atoms in one molecule. Scale by the moles.
That is the amount of CO₂. Each molecule holds more than one O atom.

questions.prompt: What is its charge now, counting each proton as +1?
hints: Each electron carries a negative charge.
At first the five positive and five negative charges cancel. What changes after three more electrons?
Which kind of charge now has the larger count, and by how many?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 positive charges against 8 negative ones leaves 5 − 8 = −3.

questions.onCorrect: −3. Three extra electrons leave three units of negative charge. This is an ion, and its charge is protons minus electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Extra electrons make the atom negative.
That counts the electrons. Charge compares them with the protons.

questions.prompt: Why is the charge positive when there are more protons than electrons?

acceptedIdeas: Protons carry positive charge, so the surplus protons leave a net positive charge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each unmatched proton leaves +1 uncancelled.

choices.label: Protons carry positive charge, so the surplus protons leave a net positive charge
Protons are heavier than electrons
Electrons only count when the atom is neutral

questions.onCorrect: Right: charges cancel in pairs, and the unmatched protons are what remain.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is not what sets charge. Each proton carries +1.
Electrons always count. Each one carries −1.

questions.prompt: A calcium ion has 20 protons and 18 electrons. What is its charge?
hints: Which is larger, the proton count or the electron count?
Subtract the electrons from the protons.
Keep the sign of the result.
questions.onCorrect: +2. More protons than electrons, by two, makes a 2+ ion.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Protons outnumber electrons here.
That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom with 20 protons loses 2 electrons. How many electrons does the ion have?
hints: How many electrons does the neutral atom start with?
Neutral means electrons equal protons.
Take the lost electrons away from the starting count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Neutral: 20 electrons. After losing 2 there are 20 − 2 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Start from the neutral count and take away what was lost.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds electrons. The atom lost some.
That is the charge of the ion, not its electron count.

questions.prompt: How many more neutrons does the second atom have?
hints: Both are carbon. What does that tell you about their protons?
If the protons match, where must the extra nucleus particles be?
Take the smaller nucleus count from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both carbon atoms have the same protons, so the extra 14 − 12 = 2 particles are neutrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Same protons, so the whole difference is in the neutrons. Atoms like these have a name, which comes next.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second nucleus's total, not how many more it has.
That adds the two nuclei. Compare them instead.

questions.prompt: Why do we subtract the atomic number from the mass number?

acceptedIdeas: The mass number includes the protons, so taking them away leaves the neutrons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A = Z + N, so N = A − Z.

choices.label: The mass number includes the protons, so taking them away leaves the neutrons
The atomic number counts the electrons, which must be removed
Subtraction always gives the lighter isotope

questions.onCorrect: Right: A holds protons and neutrons, so subtracting Z leaves N.

misconceptions.feedback: The atomic number counts protons, and electrons are not in the mass number.
The subtraction finds neutrons in one atom. It does not compare isotopes.

questions.prompt: Potassium-41 has atomic number 19. How many neutrons does it have?
hints: The mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
How many of those are protons?
Take the atomic number off the mass number.
questions.onCorrect: 22. Mass number minus atomic number leaves the neutrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass number. It still includes the protons.
That adds the atomic number. Take the protons away instead.

questions.prompt: A sample has equal numbers of atoms of mass 12 u and 14 u. Where does its average mass lie?

acceptedIdeas: Between 12 u and 14 u
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An average of two values lies between them.

choices.label: Between 12 u and 14 u
Exactly 12 u
Above 14 u

questions.onCorrect: An average of different masses lies between the lightest and heaviest.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the atoms are heavier than that, so the average is pulled up.
No atom is heavier than 14 u, so the average cannot be either.

questions.prompt: Neon-20 and neon-22 are isotopes of one element. How many more neutrons does neon-22 have?
hints: Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons.
So the difference in mass number is a difference in what?
Subtract the smaller mass number from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Same protons, so the extra 22 − 20 = 2 particles are neutrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Isotopes share protons, so the mass numbers differ only by neutrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass number of neon-22. The question asks for the difference.
That adds the mass numbers. Compare them instead.
That is the neutron count of neon-22. The question asks how many more it has.

questions.prompt: How many −2 cards make a winning hand with one +6 card?
hints: The total must be zero. How much negative score do you need?
Each −2 card supplies a fixed amount of that.
Divide the score you need to cancel by the score of one card.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The −2 cards must total −6, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cards.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The positive and negative scores have to cancel. Ions in a compound are balanced in just the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the score to cancel, not the number of cards.
Two −2 cards total −4, which is not enough.
Four −2 cards total −8, which overshoots.

questions.prompt: Why is the formula Na₂S rather than NaS?

acceptedIdeas: One Na⁺ only cancels half of the sulfide ion's charge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two +1 charges cancel one −2 charge.

choices.label: One Na⁺ only cancels half of the sulfide ion's charge
Sulfur always has a subscript of 1
Sodium atoms are smaller than sulfur atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: the subscripts are chosen so that the charges add to zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The subscript on S is 1 because one sulfide ion is enough. The count of Na⁺ comes from the charge.
Size does not set the ratio. Charge does.

questions.prompt: Ca²⁺ and N³⁻ form a neutral compound. What is the smallest number of Ca²⁺ ions in the simplest formula?
hints: Find the smallest total charge that both +2 and −3 divide into.
That total is the same size on both sides.
Divide it by the charge on one calcium ion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three Ca²⁺ give +6 and two N³⁻ give −6, so 3 calcium ions.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Three Ca²⁺ (+6) balance two N³⁻ (−6), the smallest whole-number match.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of nitride ions. The question asks about calcium.
That is the charge to balance, not the number of ions.

questions.prompt: Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ form Fe₂O₃. How many ions are in one formula unit altogether?
hints: Read the two subscripts.
A subscript counts the ions of that kind.
Add the two counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 + 3 = 5 ions.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The subscripts count the ions of each kind, so add them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the subscripts. Add them to count the ions.
That is only the iron ions. Count the oxide ions as well.

questions.prompt: How many people are in the second row?
hints: Which row fills first, and how many does it take?
Take those people off the total.
Do the remaining people fit in the second row, or do they spill into the third?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 people remain, and the second row holds up to 8, so all 7 sit there.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The front row fills first and the rest go to the next row. Electrons fill shells in the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is everyone. The first row takes some of them.
That is how many the second row could hold. Only the people left over sit there.

questions.prompt: A neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons. How many are in its second shell?
hints: Which shell fills first, and how many does it take?
Take those electrons off the total.
Does the second shell have room for all the rest?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 − 2 = 4, and the second shell holds up to 8.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The first shell takes 2, and the rest fit in the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every electron. Two are in the first shell.
That is the first shell. The question asks about the second.

questions.prompt: Why do the last 4 electrons of silicon go into a third shell?

acceptedIdeas: The second shell holds eight at most, so it is already full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 + 8 = 10 electrons fill the first two shells, so 4 must go further out.

choices.label: The second shell holds eight at most, so it is already full
Electrons prefer to be far from the nucleus
The third shell is always filled first

questions.onCorrect: Right: once a shell is full the next electrons go into the shell outside it.

misconceptions.feedback: Electrons fill the inner shells first. The outer shell gets what is left.
Shells fill from the inside, so the third is filled last.

questions.prompt: After filling the first shell with 2 and the second with 8, how many of magnesium's 12 electrons are left?
hints: Add up the electrons in the first two shells.
Take that total off the 12.
What is left is in the third shell.
questions.onCorrect: 2. The electrons left after the inner shells are the valence electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what is left after the first shell only. Fill the second as well.
That is the second shell's share. The question asks for what is left over.

questions.prompt: A neutral beryllium atom has 4 electrons. How many valence electrons does it have?
hints: How many electrons fit in the first shell?
Take those off the total.
Is there a second shell with electrons in it?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 − 2 = 2 left for the second shell, which is the last one used.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The first shell takes two, and the rest are the outer electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every electron. Some are in the inner shell.
That is the capacity of the second shell, not how many electrons sit in it.

questions.prompt: How many eggs do 20 pancakes need?
hints: How many pancakes does one egg make?
Then find how many eggs 20 pancakes need.
Divide 20 by the pancakes per egg, or scale the recipe.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 eggs make 8 pancakes, so one egg makes four. Then 20 ÷ 4 = 5 eggs.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A ratio scales: the same proportion holds for more or fewer. An equation's coefficients are a ratio like this.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the eggs by 5 without checking the ratio. Find how many eggs each pancake needs.
That multiplies the eggs by the pancakes. Use the ratio instead.

questions.prompt: In 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃, how many moles of Fe react with 3 mol of O₂?
hints: Read the coefficient in front of Fe.
The coefficients are a ratio in moles.
The O₂ coefficient matches the 3 mol you have, so the amounts match the coefficients.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficients are 4 for Fe and 3 for O₂, so 3 mol O₂ goes with 4 mol Fe.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The coefficients are the mole ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount of O₂. The coefficient of Fe is different.
That is the Fe₂O₃ coefficient. The question asks about iron.

questions.prompt: Why is Na written underneath in the conversion factor?

acceptedIdeas: So the moles of Na cancel and the answer is in moles of Cl₂
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Na on the bottom cancels the Na on top.

choices.label: So the moles of Na cancel and the answer is in moles of Cl₂
Because sodium has the larger coefficient
Because the factor must always have the smaller number on top

questions.onCorrect: Right: put the unit you have underneath so it cancels and leaves the unit you want.

misconceptions.feedback: The position follows the units, not which coefficient is larger.
There is no rule about which number is larger. The units decide.

questions.prompt: For 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, how many moles of O₂ are needed for 6 mol of Mg?
hints: Compare the O₂ coefficient with the Mg coefficient.
There is one O₂ for every two Mg.
Multiply 6 by that ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 × 1/2 = 3 mol of O₂.

questions.onCorrect: 3 mol. One O₂ goes with each two Mg, so halve the magnesium amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount, but the ratio is one O₂ for every two Mg.
That is the magnesium amount. Scale it by the ratio.

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of H₂ are needed to make 4 mol of NH₃?
hints: Which two coefficients matter here?
Three H₂ go with two NH₃.
Multiply 4 by the ratio of H₂ to NH₃.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 × 3/2 = 6 mol of H₂.

questions.onCorrect: 6 mol. The ratio is three H₂ for every two NH₃.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount, but the ratio of H₂ to NH₃ is not two to one.
That is the ammonia amount. Scale it by the ratio.

questions.prompt: How many slices of bread are in the 5 boxes?
hints: How much bread is in one box?
Each box has the same amount.
Multiply the bread in one box by the number of boxes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 boxes × 2 slices = 10 slices.

questions.onCorrect: 10. One box's contents times the number of boxes. A formula with a number in front works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bread in one box. You bought more than one.
That adds the numbers. Multiply the bread in one box by the boxes.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of CH₄?
hints: Find the small number after the H.
That is the subscript, and it counts that element's atoms.
There is one molecule, so nothing else multiplies it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The subscript after H is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The subscript after H counts the hydrogen atoms in one molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon, which has no subscript. The question asks about hydrogen.
That counts every atom. The question asks about hydrogen only.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the subscript by the coefficient?

acceptedIdeas: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms in one unit times the units gives all the atoms.

choices.label: The coefficient says how many units there are, and each unit has that many atoms
